steps: Choose the grape material
Use white grapes and decide which solids will remain with the juice. The presence of stems is a separate choice.
Manage contact
Keep juice or fermenting wine with the grape material for the intended period. Extraction changes colour and structure.
Separate when appropriate
Press or rack the wine from the solids according to the chosen method. Longer contact is not automatically a quality advantage.
Evaluate the finished style
Check tannin, acidity, aroma and any developed character. Describe the actual bottle rather than assuming every amber wine tastes alike.
traps: Not every qvevri wine is orange.
Orange does not certify organic or sulphur-free production.
Amber colour does not prove deliberate oxidation.
where: Kakheti
Georgian traditions include extended contact with grape material in qvevri, with substantial extraction in some styles.
Imereti
Georgian regional methods differ in their handling of grape material; do not turn one Kakhetian example into a rule for all qvevri wine.
skin-contact-orange.why: A guest expecting a familiar crisp white may be surprised by tannin. Explain the texture before recommending the wine: a white grape treated with extended skin contact can feel more structured. For a Brennan's training comparison, consider whether a dish has enough richness or savoury depth to work with that texture, then taste the combination. This is a learning hypothesis, not a house pairing claim. Ask about the guest's interest in unfamiliar styles without calling the wine better or more authentic than conventional white wine. Report observed aromas clearly and separate deliberate style from a genuine fault.

deeper.head: Water storage and drainage coexist
deeper.text: A vineyard can retain useful moisture and still allow excess water to move away. The question is which pores hold water and which permit air and drainage, together with the depth available to roots. Texture provides clues, but structure and compaction can alter behaviour. Avoid teaching that every clay soil is waterlogged or every stony soil is drought-proof.

deeper.head: Nutrition is not rock flavour
deeper.text: Vines take up dissolved mineral nutrients needed for growth. That biological requirement does not mean a wine's aroma is a dissolved version of its parent rock. Minerality is a varied sensory vocabulary, and its causes remain debated. Describe a flinty aroma, chalk-like texture or saline impression precisely, without turning those words into proof of geological origin.

deeper.head: Soil chemistry and wine chemistry
deeper.text: Soil pH influences nutrient availability and plant health, but it is not interchangeable with wine pH. Grape composition, vine function, harvest choices and winemaking intervene between the two. A high-pH vineyard soil does not provide a shortcut for predicting a low-acid glass, just as a limestone label does not supply a laboratory measurement of wine acidity.

deeper.head: Build a defensible terroir explanation
deeper.text: For an unfamiliar vineyard, ask for a soil profile, seasonal water observations and relevant vine measurements before concluding why it performs as it does. Compare climate, rootstock, crop and harvest choices as well. A convincing terroir account links measurable conditions to plausible effects, recognises interacting causes and leaves room for uncertainty instead of assigning a guaranteed flavour to a rock name.

exam: Distinguish texture, structure and effective rooting depth.
Explain why drainage and water storage are different.
Separate a mineral tasting descriptor from a claim about its cause.
soils-drainage.how: Study the soil profile rather than only its surface. Texture describes the proportions of mineral particle sizes; structure describes how particles form aggregates and pore spaces. These features, along with depth and compaction, affect water movement and root access. A compact layer or shallow bedrock can restrict rooting even where the topsoil looks suitable. Roots require oxygen, so persistent waterlogging creates a different problem from a useful reserve of stored water. Nutrient availability also depends on soil chemistry and biological processes. The grower assesses the actual site, selects suitable plant material and manages traffic, cover and water accordingly. For a wine explanation, connect these conditions to vine growth and ripening, then acknowledge the additional effects of climate and cellar decisions.
soils-drainage.law: A soil description is not a universal classification of wine quality. Appellation rules may define geography or specified production conditions, but words such as volcanic, limestone or gravelly do not carry one worldwide sensory guarantee. Use the local specification for legal claims and the vineyard evidence for physical descriptions.

steps: Inspect the profile
Consider effective rooting depth, texture, structure and any compact or impermeable layer. Surface stones alone are insufficient evidence.
Track water movement
Distinguish infiltration into the surface, storage within the root zone and drainage of excess water below it.
Check root conditions
Assess aeration, nutrient availability and the fit between soil, rootstock and expected water supply before interpreting vine performance.
Explain the outcome carefully
Describe how the site may influence growth and ripening. Use mineral tasting words as observations, not a geological proof.
traps: Poor soil is not automatically superior wine soil.
Clay content alone does not determine drainage.
Soil pH is not the same measurement as wine pH.
where: Chablis
The regional wine body's explanation of minerality distinguishes dissolved nutrients used by vines from geological rocks. Its tasting vocabulary is not evidence of literal stone flavour.
British Columbia
The grower guide treats soil assessment as part of vineyard establishment, connecting the root environment with drainage, water supply and planting decisions.
soils-drainage.why: Soil knowledge improves a wine story when it replaces vague claims with a useful mechanism. A clay-rich soil may retain water, yet its drainage also depends on structure and site position. A freely draining soil may need careful water management during drought. Neither situation automatically makes better wine. In service, focus on the bottle's texture, acidity and fruit, then explain the site's contribution with proportionate confidence.

deeper.head: Living yeast changes texture
deeper.text: Flor is not simply a passive lid. Its metabolism alters wine composition, including glycerol and acetaldehyde, helping explain why a biologically aged wine can feel lean and smell pungently savoury. A flor-related aroma is meaningful in its production context, rather than automatically being treated as a fault in every wine.

deeper.head: Use the dated specification
deeper.text: The 2026 Jerez text distinguishes protected wines that reach the required strength through fermentation from liqueur wines that are fortified. It also allows vintage ageing alongside the dynamic system. Older educational pages remain helpful for cellar descriptions but cannot override the later specification on either point.

deeper.head: Two independent axes
deeper.text: Draw one axis for biological versus oxidative ageing and another for fractional blending versus a vintage system. This avoids equating solera with flor. For Amontillado, add a sequence: biological development occurs first, followed by oxidative development. That sequence explains more than calling it halfway between two unrelated styles.

deeper.head: Introduce dry Sherry without confusion
deeper.text: When a guest expects all Sherry to taste sweet, offer a clear description of the specific dry style before explaining flor. Keep dryness, nuttiness and oxidative character separate in your vocabulary. A nutty aroma does not mean added sugar. The lesson is to describe the actual bottle accurately while using the ageing history to explain, rather than replace, the tasting.

exam: Flor is living yeast; solera is fractional blending.
Amontillado combines sequential biological and oxidative ageing.
The current Jerez specification does not require every dry Sherry to be fortified.
solera-and-flor.how: A dry base wine destined for biological ageing is held with space above it, allowing flor to develop on the surface under suitable cellar conditions. The yeast changes the wine's chemistry, including consuming glycerol and producing acetaldehyde. Flor also limits direct oxidative development of the wine beneath it. Separately, a solera organises stocks into stages of maturity. Some wine is drawn from the final stage; that space is replenished from a younger stage, which is itself replenished in turn. The process preserves continuity without emptying the whole system. A producer can use fractional blending for biologically aged or oxidatively aged wines. The visible stack of barrels is only an illustration of the system, not its defining mechanism.
solera-and-flor.law: The Jerez specification consolidated under the Order of 13 May 2026 includes both wine and liqueur-wine categories. Fortification is therefore not compulsory for every protected dry Sherry. It defines Fino by exclusively biological ageing and Amontillado by biological followed by oxidative ageing. It also permits both criaderas-and-solera and vintage ageing. These current provisions take precedence over older summaries that say all Sherry is fortified or all biological ageing must use a solera.

steps: Establish the ageing environment
Choose biological or oxidative development according to the intended style. Flor requires suitable conditions and is a living yeast population.
Maintain the wine
Monitor the surface and cellar conditions for biological ageing. Without flor, oxygen influences maturation more directly.
Withdraw a fraction
Draw part of the wine from the final solera stage. A withdrawal is not the emptying of the entire oldest stock.
Replenish in sequence
Refresh each stage from a younger one. The flow between maturity stages, rather than the physical height of a barrel, defines the system.
traps: A solera can operate without flor.
The founding date is not the age of every component.
An older marketing explanation is not the latest legal specification.
where: Jerez-Xérès-Sherry
The denomination provides the principal examples here: Fino, Amontillado and Oloroso demonstrate different ageing histories.
Sanlúcar de Barrameda
Manzanilla has a separate protected designation associated with biological ageing in Sanlúcar; do not apply the Jerez Fino location rule to it.
solera-and-flor.why: At the table, explain a Fino through its dryness, savoury character and fresh handling, rather than introducing it as a sweet after-dinner drink. Explain an Amontillado as a wine that has experienced both biological and oxidative ageing. For a food discussion, compare the actual wine with salty, savoury or nutty elements in the dish, then consider intensity. These are starting points for tasting, not guaranteed matches. A solera's historical founding date is interesting storytelling, but it cannot honestly be presented as the age of every drop poured. Give the guest the style first and the cellar history second.

deeper.head: A living interface
deeper.text: Surface yeast has access to the wine below and oxygen above. Its metabolism changes compounds in the wine rather than merely stopping air at a barrier. The Sherry explanation of flor illustrates this biological principle, but the local cellar system is different from a Jura barrel. Use the comparison to understand the mechanism while preserving the identities of both traditions.

deeper.head: Nutty does not always mean faulty
deeper.text: A nutty impression may be welcome in an intentionally developed wine and disappointing in a fragile fruit-led white that has deteriorated. Start with the intended style and assess balance, freshness and the complete aroma. Do not excuse every stale or vinegary bottle by mentioning oxidation. Equally, do not reject a sound traditional wine simply because its profile differs from youthful fruit.

deeper.head: Do not transfer a timetable
deeper.text: A long producer ageing period is evidence for that wine. It does not establish the legal minimum for every sous-voile label or the exact stage from which a rule counts time. Separate the method, the designation and the vintage-specific producer account. This is especially important when search results include old specifications or proposed amendments beside current documents.

deeper.head: Offer a confident introduction
deeper.text: For a guest interested in a dry wine with savoury complexity, explain the yeast veil briefly and describe what is actually in the glass. Mushroom, cream or mature cheese preparations may provide useful starting points for a pairing discussion, but confirm the wine and dish together. Avoid promising that every sous-voile wine needs the same aeration or serving temperature.

exam: Contrast surface yeast with settled lees.
Translate ouillé and sous voile without merging them.
Distinguish a biological method from a named wine category.
sous-voile.how: After alcoholic fermentation, the cellar creates conditions in which surface yeast can develop during maturation. In a Jura sous-voile regime, barrels are not routinely topped in the same way as an ouillé wine, leaving space above the liquid. The film is biologically active and interacts with oxygen and wine components; it is not a sterile physical lid. The result depends on wine composition, the yeast population and cellar conditions. This differs from simple exposure of an unprotected wine to air and from ageing on dead yeast deposits at the bottom of a vessel. A producer may make both topped and sous-voile wines, so a regional name alone cannot tell you how every white wine was raised.
sous-voile.law: Sous voile describes a method, while named wines such as Vin Jaune carry origin-specific production conditions. A producer example demonstrates one regime, not every current appellation rule. Consult the current specification for precise ageing or grape requirements. A proposed amendment is not evidence that a new rule has taken effect.

steps: Establish the base wine
Identify the grape and completed fermentation before studying the separate maturation stage.
Manage the vessel
Follow the producer account of barrel fill, topping policy and cellar conditions instead of equating all headspace with a desirable veil.
Observe the living film
Monitor the wine and its surface development, distinguishing the intended biological regime from uncontrolled spoilage.
Assess the finished style
Taste the actual balance and aroma, then prepare a service explanation that names the style and its confirmed method.
traps: Every Jura white is not made sous voile.
A yeast veil is not a sterile airtight seal.
An intentionally nutty style does not excuse an unsound bottle.
where: Jura
Compare sous-voile and ouillé whites to understand how the topping decision and biological maturation can shape different expressions.
Château-Chalon
A documented producer example uses Savagnin and extended maturation beneath a yeast veil; keep its particular details distinct from universal requirements.
Jerez comparison
Flor-aged Sherry shows another surface-yeast system. Its local grapes, cellar organisation and production rules should not be transferred wholesale to Jura.
sous-voile.why: This method can build distinctive savoury complexity and alter texture. For a guest, the important result may be a dry wine with nutty or spicy depth rather than primary fruit alone. It is worth offering a taste where service allows, because an enthusiast of crisp fruit-led whites may not want this expression even when it is well made.

deeper.head: Three separate questions
deeper.text: Learn to name the intervention before explaining it. Fining adds an agent to interact with wine constituents; filtration passes wine through a physical barrier; sulphur dioxide provides chemical and microbial protection. They can be used together, but one is not a synonym for another. When a guest asks whether a wine was treated, replace that vague question with the specific information they need.

deeper.head: Vegan requests need evidence
deeper.text: Animal-derived fining agents include products associated with egg, milk and fish, while other agents have different origins. That distinction matters when answering a vegan request. It does not mean the final bottle contains a visibly identifiable ingredient. A reliable service answer comes from the producer or a recognised certification for that bottling, with allergy questions handled separately through the restaurant's established process.

deeper.head: Free is not total
deeper.text: A total sulphur dioxide figure includes bound material and does not reveal the whole protective situation. The balance of free forms changes with pH, and analytical methods can introduce additional complications in red wine. Evaluate the question being asked: an analytical report, a legal declaration and resistance to microbial spoilage are connected subjects, but they are not interchangeable measurements.

deeper.head: Evaluate an unfiltered claim
deeper.text: An unfiltered claim tells you that a particular separation was omitted, if the claim is accurate. It does not establish that the wine was never fined, that it lacks sulphur dioxide, or that it is more stable. In a comparative answer, explain the producer's choice and its consequences for handling, then reserve the quality judgement for the wine's balance and condition.

exam: Distinguish fining, filtration and sulphur dioxide by mechanism.
Explain why free and total sulphur dioxide answer different questions.
Describe a producer verification step for a vegan request.
stabilisation-sulphur.how: A winemaker first identifies the intended result: clearer appearance, protein stability, a change in astringency, or greater microbial security. Small fining trials compare treated samples with an untreated control before deciding whether to proceed. After suitable settling or separation, the unwanted material and fining agent are removed. Filtration is selected for its purpose; a coarse clarification stage and a validated microbial removal stage are not interchangeable. Sulphur dioxide exists in free and bound forms, with their sum reported as total. Its protective action cannot be judged from total alone, because pH and the available free fraction matter. Treatment decisions therefore combine measurement, tasting and the wine's intended route to the customer.
stabilisation-sulphur.law: Permitted substances, conditions of use and labelling obligations depend on the destination market and wine category. OIV descriptions explain recognised methods but do not replace local law. Do not infer an allergen declaration, vegan certification or exemption from a general description of fining. This lesson deliberately gives no universal sulphur limit or cellar dose.

steps: Identify the question
Separate visible haze, protein instability, unwanted harshness and microbial risk. One treatment will not necessarily answer all of them.
Compare small trials
Check a proposed fining treatment against an untreated sample. The useful endpoint is the intended improvement with the least unnecessary loss of desirable character.
Select a separation
Match filtration to the particles or organisms being targeted. A description such as filtered needs more detail before it establishes microbial stability.
Measure protection
Consider free and total sulphur dioxide alongside pH, rather than translating one total measurement into a universal protective dose.
Confirm the bottle information
For a guest asking about vegan suitability or allergens, obtain the producer's current statement for the wine. Appearance cannot establish which processing aids were used.
traps: Filtered does not necessarily mean sterilising filtration.
Unfiltered does not establish unfined or vegan status.
A universal dose cannot be inferred from total sulphur alone.
where: White wine cellars
Bentonite can be used to remove proteins associated with instability. This is a targeted treatment, rather than evidence that all white wine needs the same correction.
Red wine cellars
Some fining agents are used to modify astringency or bitterness. The choice depends on a trial with the particular wine, rather than its colour alone.
Bottling preparation
Filtration and sulphur management can form part of a stability plan. Neither word on its own describes every protection used before a wine leaves the cellar.
stabilisation-sulphur.why: These tools can help a wine reach the table in the condition its maker intended. The trade-off is that unnecessary treatment can remove desirable material or create extra handling. A clear wine is not necessarily heavily treated, and a cloudy wine is not automatically more expressive. Explain the producer's aim, then describe the wine's actual freshness, texture and balance without ranking every filtered or unfiltered bottle in advance.

deeper.head: Three layouts, different consequences
deeper.text: The Douro regulator describes the transition from narrow historic terraces to broader systems and later mechanised layouts. Patamares provide benches following the slope, whereas vinha ao alto follows the direction of largest descent. The contrast matters for machinery and runoff. A map or photograph should show the direction of rows and the supporting structure before its caption names the system.

deeper.head: Aspect is not the same as gradient
deeper.text: Gradient describes how steep the land is; aspect describes the direction it faces. An exposed slope can gain useful warmth in a cool region but impose heat and water stress in a warmer one. Altitude and wind modify that balance further. In an exam answer, state the location and objective before praising sunshine, and resist transferring a northern cool climate explanation unchanged to every hillside.

deeper.head: Heritage creates a continuing obligation
deeper.text: A terrace is an engineered part of a living landscape, not simply a decorative relic. Maintaining walls, access and drainage supports continued cultivation, while abandonment can change both the cultural landscape and water behaviour. When explaining cost, separate the effort of preserving the site from a claim about sensory superiority. The value of heritage can be real even when quality must still be judged in the glass.

deeper.head: Compare systems without romantic shortcuts
deeper.text: For two hillside wines, ask whether the parcels share aspect, soil depth, elevation, vine age and water supply. A narrow hand worked terrace and a mechanised layout may also differ in crop selection and economics. Without accounting for those factors, attributing a flavour to manual labour or terrace width is weak reasoning. Teach landscape, process and tasting evidence as connected but separate observations.

exam: Define aspect separately from gradient.
Distinguish patamares from vinha ao alto.
Explain both exposure benefits and erosion constraints.
steep-slopes.how: A grower first assesses the slope's stability, drainage routes, soil depth and exposure. Traditional stone supported terraces retain soil in narrow planting areas and may require substantial manual work. Modern earth terraces can make some operations easier, but their width, bank design and water handling must suit the terrain. In the Douro, patamares follow the hillside in terraces, while vinha ao alto aligns rows down the slope rather than across it. Those are distinct systems, not interchangeable names for any hillside vineyard. Each arrangement changes access, the usable planted area and the path taken by runoff. Surface cover and maintained drainage can help manage erosion, while damaged walls or concentrated flows can undermine the vineyard. Mechanisation depends on safe access and slope geometry; even where specialised equipment is possible, steep farming retains constraints that are absent on level ground.
steep-slopes.law: Terrace construction and hillside cultivation can be constrained by planning, heritage, environmental and appellation rules. Requirements vary with the site and the scale of alteration. A picturesque location is not permission to reshape it. Likewise, regional categories that refer to steep vineyards should be checked under their own definitions; there is no single worldwide slope threshold that establishes superior wine quality.

Vineyard landscaping in the Douro Valley, Taylor Fladgate
VDP: Mosel vineyard landscape

steps: Read the slope
Consider gradient, aspect, soil depth and drainage as separate properties before assuming that a dramatic hillside is favourable.
Choose the layout
Match terraces or row orientation to terrain and access, recognising that different systems change water movement and working space.
Maintain the structure
Inspect banks, walls and drainage after heavy weather, because a productive terrace depends on continuing care.
Explain the wine
Use the site story to describe the grower's work, then assess flavour and balance rather than awarding quality for steepness alone.
traps: Steepness does not guarantee wine quality.
Every hillside planting is not a terrace.
A cool region's preferred exposure is not a universal rule.
where: Douro
Stone supported terraces, earth patamares and vinha ao alto show several responses to rugged terrain. They differ in layout, access and the way water moves.
Mosel
Many sloping vineyards illustrate the importance of aspect and access in a cool setting. The river landscape still contains varied sites rather than one uniform exposure.
steep-slopes.why: Favourable exposure can aid ripening in cool conditions, while drainage and soil depth affect water supply. In warm regions, a cooler aspect may be more useful than maximum sunshine. Steep sites can also be thin, dry or difficult to manage. At the table, the labour and landscape can explain part of a wine's story and cost, but they do not guarantee intensity or longevity. Compare actual acidity, tannin and development before recommending a bottle with a dish.

deeper.head: A label and a process
deeper.text: Learn the process first: wine remains with suitable lees. Then learn the local label conditions as an additional layer. This prevents two errors: assuming any lees-aged wine qualifies for a particular designation, and assuming wines without those words never rested on lees. A technical sheet and an appellation specification answer different questions and should be read together.

deeper.head: Dates belong to a designation
deeper.text: An exact bottling window is a legal detail that needs a named appellation and a current source. When teaching a general method, it is more accurate to explain why the condition matters than to spread one date across several names. The key distinction is between cellar contact, permission to use wording and release of the finished wine. They need not describe the same event.

deeper.head: Freshness with a fuller middle
deeper.text: A wine can be dry and lively yet have a rounded texture. Avoid presenting these as opposing states. During a comparative tasting, note the attack, middle and finish separately, and then consult production information. If the wine feels broader than expected, lees contact is a possible explanation, but grape composition and other cellar choices still belong in the account.

deeper.head: Build a useful service sentence
deeper.text: For shellfish or a delicate seafood preparation, a helpful description might begin with a dry, fresh white and a little extra texture through the middle. Only then add the verified lees-ageing detail. Taste the wine and consider the sauce before promising a match. Shellfish on its own and shellfish with a rich cream sauce may call for different balances.

exam: Translate sur lie accurately.
Distinguish generic lees contact from label eligibility.
Read the full Muscadet designation before quoting rules.
sur-lie.how: In a lees-aged still wine, suitable fine sediment remains in contact with the wine after fermentation. The producer monitors that contact and may choose to stir, although stirring is not built into the definition of sur lie. A Muscadet label must be read as an origin-specific statement rather than a generic recipe. Appellation conditions can address the period of lees contact and where or when bottling occurs. For learning, separate the broad meaning of the French words from the detailed rule applying to the particular appellation. Also separate the technical process from the tasting result: different vineyards, vintages and cellar choices can produce distinct textures even where the same expression appears on the bottle.
sur-lie.law: INAO describes specific fine-lees and bottling conditions for Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie. Those conditions belong to that designation and should be checked in its current specification when exact dates matter. The generic meaning of sur lie does not impose the same timetable on every wine worldwide.

sources.title: Lees ageing in Muscadet, Vins de Nantes
Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie, INAO
Enology Notes 25: yeast lees, Virginia Tech

steps: Read the full name
Identify the appellation and exact label wording rather than interpreting sur lie on its own.
Confirm the contact
Look for the producer account of fine lees, vessel and duration, noting whether stirring is actually mentioned.
Check the rule
Use the current appellation specification for dates or bottling conditions; do not borrow a rule from another Muscadet designation.
Taste and describe
Assess dryness, acidity, body and texture before explaining how lees contact may contribute to the wine.
traps: Sur lie does not mean sweet.
Lees contact does not require new oak or stirring.
One appellation timetable is not a worldwide rule.
where: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine
An essential place to connect the label expression with a dry still white wine and its origin-specific production conditions.
Other Muscadet designations
Compare the full appellation name before assuming that wording, timing or release conditions are identical.
Wider cellar vocabulary
A producer elsewhere may describe lees ageing in technical notes without using a protected Muscadet label expression.
sur-lie.why: This term is valuable because it links a cellar method with an easily recognisable label. It can help a guest understand why a fresh white has a rounded middle or subtle savoury character. It should not become a shortcut that replaces tasting. A producer-confirmed account gives the explanation credibility without implying every bottle tastes alike.

deeper.head: Pressure is retained through bottling
deeper.text: The gas comes from yeast activity, but it must be conserved when the wine leaves its fermentation vessel. Pressure controlled transfer and filling help maintain the finished effervescence. This explains why fermentation location and bottling operation are distinct questions. If a guest asks whether the bubbles are artificial, describe the wine's actual production process rather than assuming that anything made in a tank is carbonated by injection.

deeper.head: Method and sweetness are separate
deeper.text: Fruit aromas can create an impression of sweetness even when a wine tastes relatively dry. Conversely, crisp acidity and carbon dioxide can make residual sugar feel less obvious. Compare the tasting result with the label category. Extra Dry in the sparkling vocabulary is sweeter than Brut, despite everyday English suggesting otherwise. Teach that contrast before using a bottle to recommend a pairing, especially for a guest seeking a dry aperitif.

deeper.head: One tank, different fermentation pathways
deeper.text: Draw separate diagrams for a base wine given a second fermentation and grape must whose first fermentation is controlled to preserve sugar. Both can use pressure tanks, yet their starting material and sweetness management differ. The distinction prevents the common shortcut that every sparkling wine ferments twice. The question to ask is what entered the tank and what was still fermentable, not simply whether stainless steel was used.

deeper.head: A clearer aperitif conversation
deeper.text: When a guest asks for something dry and fruity, confirm both parts of the request. Fruity can mean an aroma preference, while dry concerns perceived sweetness. Offer a bottle whose actual balance fits, then explain the tank method only if it helps. That sequence keeps a production lesson from obscuring the guest's immediate drinking preference.

exam: Identify the second fermentation vessel in the Charmat sequence.
Distinguish fermentation gas from injected carbonation.
Contrast Prosecco's usual sequence with the Asti approach.
tank-method.how: Make the base wine and assemble the blend, then introduce yeast and fermentable sugar in a tank designed to retain pressure. Temperature and fermentation are controlled to reach the desired style. The wine can remain in contact with yeast according to the producer's approach, then is clarified or filtered and bottled while retaining its dissolved carbon dioxide. Pressure management matters through transfer and filling, rather than only during fermentation. This sequence differs from injecting gas into still wine. It also differs from the Asti approach, where grape must can undergo one controlled fermentation in tank instead of starting with a completed dry base wine. The vessel alone does not tell you the fermentation sequence.
tank-method.law: Prosecco is a protected geographic name with its own specification, not the general name for tank fermented wine. Its consortium describes the Martinotti or Charmat method for sparkling production. Other sparkling categories and appellations have different rules. Asti and Moscato d'Asti also require their own study: using a pressure tank does not make their fermentation identical to Prosecco's.

steps: Prepare the base
Select and blend wines for fruit, acidity and the intended finished balance.
Retain fermentation gas
Carry out the second fermentation in a closed pressure tank with controlled temperature.
Assess and finish
Manage lees contact, clarity and final sweetness for the specified wine style.
Bottle under pressure
Transfer and fill while maintaining conditions that preserve the dissolved carbon dioxide.
traps: A pressure tank does not automatically mean two fermentations.
Tank method does not mean poor quality or no lees contact.
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut in sparkling terminology.
where: Veneto and Friuli
Prosecco DOC illustrates the tank method's role in preserving the expression of Glera and the selected blend.
Piedmont
Asti is a useful contrast because its tank process can retain grape sugar during a single fermentation of must.
tank-method.why: For aromatic or delicate grapes, a relatively direct route from base wine to bottle can keep primary fruit prominent. Longer contact with lees is possible, so tank method does not mean that all yeast influence is absent. At the table, offer fruit and floral descriptors only when they fit the wine. A useful comparison is fresh pear and blossom against a more savoury bottle matured sparkling style, while acknowledging overlap.

deeper.head: Tirage, dosage and the tasting sequence
deeper.text: Reconstruct the sequence when a guest asks whether the wine has added sugar. Sugar supplied at tirage feeds the second fermentation; the yeast converts it rather than simply leaving it as sweetness. Dosage is a later adjustment. A low dosage therefore tells you little about the amount originally needed to develop pressure, and it does not prove that the grapes were less ripe. Ask which stage a technical figure describes before comparing producers.

deeper.head: Autolysis is one contributor
deeper.text: Lees maturation is more than a stopwatch. The breakdown of yeast cells interacts with the wine, while its earlier fermentation, reserve wine content and handling also influence texture and aroma. Bread or toast in a tasting note is a useful association, not proof of an exact ageing period. A strong training answer connects a plausible mechanism to an observed character and then states what the glass alone cannot establish.

deeper.head: Separate evidence from prestige
deeper.text: Compare two sparkling wines by origin, fermentation vessel, time on lees, dosage and condition at service. Do not conclude that the traditional method must be superior to tank fermentation for every grape or purpose. Its cellar sequence offers different opportunities, but a guest may prefer immediate fruit expression. Describe the observed wine first, use the method to explain it second, and keep specific vintage or disgorgement claims tied to that bottle's technical information.

deeper.head: Comparing two sparkling bottles
deeper.text: Put a fresh, citrus-led bottle beside a more savoury example and describe each without seeing its label. Then compare the documented grape blend, lees duration and dosage. This exercise separates what you observed from what you learned afterwards. It also gives you two useful guest descriptions without claiming that flavour alone proved an exact production history.

exam: Sequence base wine, tirage, second fermentation, lees ageing, riddling, disgorgement and finishing.
Distinguish tirage sugar from dosage and sweetness.
Compare the method with tank and ancestral fermentation.
traditional-method.how: First make and assess the still base wines, then assemble the desired blend. At tirage, wine, sugar and yeast are introduced before pressure resistant bottles are closed. Yeast consumes the added sugar and releases carbon dioxide that dissolves in the wine. After fermentation, the bottles mature on their lees. Riddling gradually collects the sediment at the closure; disgorgement expels it. The bottle is topped up and, where chosen, an expedition liqueur adjusts the finished balance before final closure. Dosage belongs near the end of this sequence, whereas tirage starts the second fermentation. Neither term means fortification. The producer's ageing choices and base wine character remain important alongside the shared method.
traditional-method.law: Champagne has its own protected origin and production rules; using the traditional method elsewhere does not confer the Champagne name. Its official guidance distinguishes minimum maturation before release from a general description of lees ageing. Do not transplant Champagne's requirements to Cava, Crémant or other regions: each appellation controls its own production and release conditions.

steps: Base wine
Ferment the grape juice and select sound base wines with the balance required for the intended sparkling style.
Tirage
Introduce the yeast and fermentable sugar, then close the appropriate bottle so fermentation gas can be retained.
Lees maturation
Allow contact with the spent yeast; its duration and the base wine influence the eventual sensory result.
Riddle and disgorge
Gather the sediment near the closure and expel it while limiting wine loss.
Finish
Set the final balance, close the bottle and allow the wine to settle before service.
traps: Traditional method is not a synonym for Champagne.
Dosage does not generate the original second fermentation.
Toast aromas do not reveal an exact number of months on lees.
where: Champagne
Bottle fermentation and maturation form part of a protected regional identity, alongside geographic and vineyard rules.
Bourgogne
Crémant de Bourgogne provides another regional example of bottle fermented sparkling wine with its own specification.
traditional-method.why: The retained fermentation gas gives effervescence, while lees ageing can add breadth and breadlike or savoury notes. These are possible expressions, not compulsory aromas in every bottle. A guest who likes citrus and freshness may prefer a different example from one seeking toast and richness. Taste sweetness separately from ripeness: ripe fruit aromas do not establish residual sugar. With food, compare the wine's acidity, body and sweetness to the sauce and cooking method.

deeper.head: Cane versus cordon
deeper.text: The distinction is structural and temporal. A cane is last season's matured growth, while a cordon is older framework. A spur is a shortened piece of cane, rather than a separate woody species. Trace the sequence from bud to shoot to cane and back to retained buds. Once that cycle is clear, a winter vineyard photograph becomes easier to interpret.

deeper.head: Positioning is another choice
deeper.text: Vertical shoot positioning describes an arrangement of growing shoots, commonly supported by catch wires. It does not, on its own, tell you whether the vine was cane-pruned or spur-pruned. Use two questions when reading a technical sheet: what wood was retained during pruning, and how is new growth arranged during the season? This prevents confusing a canopy arrangement with a pruning method.

deeper.head: Fit the local conditions
deeper.text: A training decision involves constraints as well as tradition. Vigour, cultivar behaviour, growing conditions and the practical work of the vineyard shape what is suitable. Cold-climate guidance also needs to account for damaged buds or framework after winter. Compare the problem a system solves before comparing its appearance, and avoid exporting a regional recommendation unchanged to a very different vineyard.

deeper.head: Keep the causal chain intact
deeper.text: A useful explanation runs from retained buds to growth distribution and management, then to the fruit the site can ripen. It does not jump from a named system straight to a tasting note. If asked whether fewer buds produce better wine, discuss vine balance and the response of the season. The premise is too broad to support an automatic quality ranking.

exam: Distinguish a cane, a spur and a cordon.
Separate annual pruning from shoot positioning and trellis hardware.
Explain why vine condition matters when deciding what to retain.
training-pruning.how: A cane is a shoot that has matured into woody growth after a season. Fruiting shoots typically arise from buds on this retained wood. Cane pruning keeps selected longer canes while replacing the previous fruiting wood; spur pruning cuts selected canes back to short sections with a small number of buds. These spurs often sit along older cordons. A cordon is a continuing arm of the vine, not the same thing as the short spur it supports. The grower chooses a system with the cultivar, vine vigour, site and available labour in mind, then adjusts the annual pruning decision to the actual vine.
training-pruning.law: Some appellations prescribe permitted pruning forms and additional limits. Comité Champagne identifies Chablis, Cordon, Guyot and Vallée de la Marne systems, illustrating that one region may use several approaches. That does not make every version interchangeable for every grape or site. Consult the current local specification for an exact legal question; this lesson gives no worldwide bud count or pruning calendar.

steps: Read the structure
Identify trunk, older arms and last season's canes before naming the system. Distinguish the living vine from the posts and wires supporting it.
Assess the vine
Consider vigour, health and any winter injury. A weak or damaged vine should not automatically receive the same bud load as a vigorous neighbour.
Select retained wood
Choose the canes or short spurs that will carry the next season's buds, while preserving options for renewal.
Arrange the growing space
Position retained wood within the chosen framework. Later shoot positioning manages new growth rather than replacing the dormant pruning decision.
Review the season
Compare the intended crop and canopy with what developed. Learning from the response is more informative than treating a system's name as a guarantee of fruit quality.
traps: A cordon and a cane are different ages of wood.
Vertical shoot positioning does not specify one pruning method.
The smallest crop is not automatically a balanced crop.
where: Champagne
Several named systems coexist. The official regional explanation relates pruning choice to vine vigour, fertility and the need for renewal, rather than describing one universal form.
Pennsylvania vineyard education
Cane and spur pruning are taught alongside different training arrangements. These examples help separate annual retained wood from the framework carrying it.
Cold-climate vineyards
Winter injury can change which buds and wood remain useful. Regional guidance considers recovery and vine condition instead of assuming an undamaged structure every year.
training-pruning.why: A well-matched system helps the grower distribute growth, manage light and airflow, and perform vineyard work. The aim is a workable balance between vine capacity and crop, not the smallest possible number of buds. Training photographs make useful study tools: describe what each piece of wood does before memorising a regional name. This supports a more precise explanation of how a producer adapts farming to local conditions.

deeper.head: Interruption versus preservation
deeper.text: Mutage stops alcoholic fermentation by raising alcohol through spirit addition. Protecting the finished wine from oxygen is a separate decision. A wine can therefore share the same fortification principle with another example while taking a very different maturation path. Treat these as two stages when constructing a comparison.

deeper.head: Colour and ageing vocabulary
deeper.text: Rivesaltes Grenat is associated with fruit-preserving handling, while Ambré and Tuilé offer developed oxidative profiles. These names help organise a tasting, but they do not remove the need to inspect the particular bottle. Describe observed fruit and maturity rather than inferring every aroma from a colour term.

deeper.head: Natural is not unfortified
deeper.text: The category's name refers to retained grape sweetness within a defined production tradition. It does not mean the wine lacks added alcohol, nor does it certify organic viticulture. Compare VDN with a late-harvest wine by identifying how sugar was retained, not by deciding that one sounds more natural than the other.

deeper.head: Compare two sweet-wine stories
deeper.text: Present a hypothetical fruit-preserving Muscat de Rivesaltes beside a developed oxidative Rivesaltes. Both can be sweet and fortified, yet they may suit different flavour preferences. Build separate descriptions from grape expression and maturation, then test the pairing with the actual dish. This teaches a useful replacement for the unhelpful statement that both bottles are simply dessert wine.

exam: Mutage interrupts fermentation with grape spirit.
Naturel does not mean unfortified or organic.
Identify fruit-preserving versus oxidative maturation.
vin-doux-naturel.how: Grapes are fermented according to the intended wine style. During fermentation, the producer adds neutral grape spirit to stop yeast activity before all the grape sugar has been converted into alcohol. This operation is called mutage. The resulting wine can be handled to protect fresh fruit aromas or matured with deliberate oxygen exposure. Red and white varieties provide different starting materials, and wines from the same regional family can develop very different characters. A young Muscat example is therefore not a sensory model for every VDN. Confirm the actual appellation and style on the bottle, rather than relying on a broad translation such as naturally sweet wine.
vin-doux-naturel.law: VDN is a regulated category, not a casual synonym for every sweet wine. Individual appellations define their grapes and production conditions. In Roussillon, Rivesaltes, Muscat de Rivesaltes and Maury Doux provide examples. Maury also produces dry wines, so the place name alone is insufficient to identify the sweet fortified style. Do not attach a universal ageing requirement to all VDNs.

steps: Identify the intended style
Establish the grapes, colour and appellation. Muscat-based and Grenache-based wines need not share the same aroma profile.
Begin fermentation
Allow yeast to convert part of the grape sugar into alcohol. The winemaker follows the evolving balance.
Carry out mutage
Add neutral grape spirit during fermentation to retain some natural grape sugar. The sweetness does not prove that fermentation never began.
Choose maturation
Protect fruit character or allow deliberate oxidative development according to the style. These paths affect the tableside description.
traps: Maury can identify dry as well as sweet wines.
Not every VDN is aged oxidatively.
Muscat de Rivesaltes and Rivesaltes are separate appellations.
where: Rivesaltes
The appellation includes different colour and maturation styles, so the label's additional style information matters.
Muscat de Rivesaltes
Muscat varieties provide a distinct aromatic basis; it should not be confused with every wine carrying the Rivesaltes place name.
Maury Doux
Sweet fortified wines must be distinguished from the dry wines also associated with Maury.
vin-doux-naturel.why: A useful service explanation is that fermentation was stopped with grape spirit, preserving natural grape sweetness. Follow with the actual style: fresh and floral, dark-fruited, or developed and nutty, as appropriate. For a dessert recommendation, compare the wine with the sweetness, fruit and roasted flavours on the plate. A fruit-focused Muscat and an oxidative Rivesaltes offer different teaching comparisons. Neither is a universal answer to every dessert. Ask the guest whether they enjoy fresh fruit or developed flavours, and verify the particular wine before claiming a specific grape blend or ageing method.

deeper.head: Two processes in one vessel
deeper.text: Treat the tank as a changing mixture rather than a single fermentation mode. Free juice supports yeast fermentation while berries that remain intact follow a different early pathway. Crushing and pressing alter that balance. When comparing technical sheets, ask when berries were broken, how the cap was worked and whether the wine finished fermenting after pressing. These questions explain more than the headline whole-bunch percentage.

deeper.head: Test the stem assumption
deeper.text: A woody stem appearance is useful information, but it is not a tasting guarantee. Fruit composition, stem quantity and extraction conditions all influence the outcome. In a comparative tasting, separate an attractive fresh herbal note from drying bitterness or a green aroma that overwhelms fruit. Judge the combination in the glass before deciding that stems either improved or damaged the wine.

deeper.head: Evidence before attribution
deeper.text: A red wine with spice and a lifted perfume could reflect several grape and cellar factors. Build a cautious explanation: describe the observation, identify whole bunch as one possible cause, and state the production evidence needed to confirm it. Compare wines from a controlled trial where possible. Two unrelated commercial bottles can illustrate styles, but cannot isolate the effect of stems.

deeper.head: A tableside comparison
deeper.text: For a guest choosing a red with a savoury dish, translate the method into a question about preference: would they enjoy a fragrant wine with an herbal edge, or a more direct fruit expression? Then select from wines you have tasted. Never promise that whole bunch makes a wine lighter, softer or better with food. Offer a small taste when service permits.

exam: Separate whole-bunch fermentation from whole-bunch pressing.
Explain intact berries and free juice together.
Connect stem inclusion to possible aroma and texture changes.
whole-bunch.how: After sorting, the winemaker decides how much fruit to retain as complete clusters and how to arrange it with any destemmed fruit. Pressure from grapes above and subsequent cap handling release juice. Yeasts ferment that juice, while intact berries may undergo intracellular changes before they split. Stems also interact with the liquid and affect movement through the cap. The balance changes as fermentation advances, so a percentage alone does not describe the process. Whole-bunch fermentation differs from whole-bunch pressing, which extracts juice from intact clusters before a white or sparkling wine fermentation. It also differs from deliberately conducting pure carbonic maceration in a carbon dioxide atmosphere. A producer can combine aspects of these approaches, but the terms should remain separate.
whole-bunch.law: Whole bunch describes a cellar choice, not a quality tier or a universal certification. Appellation and production rules still apply to the wine. Neither a claimed percentage nor the method alone establishes an ageing category, geographical origin or eligibility for a particular label.

steps: Select the fruit
Inspect bunch health, berry condition and stems; a damaged or diseased cluster can change the suitability of the entire lot.
Choose the proportion
Retain whole clusters for a reason, then record the proportion and whether they sit above, below or among destemmed fruit.
Manage contact
Follow temperature, fermentation progress and taste as berries break. Adjust handling rather than applying an identical schedule to every tank.
Press and finish
Assess press fractions separately and check for newly released sugar from intact berries before deciding fermentation has finished.
traps: Whole bunch does not mean pure carbonic maceration.
A green aroma alone cannot prove stem inclusion.
A higher whole-bunch percentage does not establish higher quality.
where: Pinot Noir
AWRI trials use Pinot Noir to demonstrate how whole clusters can change a wine; the result belongs to the fruit and treatment, not every Pinot Noir.
Shiraz
Whole-bunch Shiraz is a useful comparison with destemmed Shiraz. Ask whether stems, intact berries or both were the intended influence.
whole-bunch.why: The aim may be aromatic lift, a different tannin shape or a less uniform extraction pattern. Stems can also help liquid drain during pressing. These advantages come with trade-offs, including unwanted green character or coarse texture. For a guest, describe the actual wine first. Explain whole bunch as a possible contributor only when the producer confirms its use.
